query: For as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles? Earlier work focused mainly on arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons, where an ordered single-phase hexagonal state undergoes a first-order magnetostructural transition that produces a large but sharp and hysteretic entropy change; these bulk forms also have limited heat-exchange rates because of their low surface-to-volume ratio. Prior searches have largely emphasized composition-dependent changes in transition temperature or response amplitude, with most studies pursuing only one optimization variable. Under the constraints of avoiding rare-earth elements, retaining mechanical stability and low cost, enabling rapid heat exchange, and limiting hysteretic losses, specify one controlled intervention that would distinguish the proposed governing explanation from alternatives, the predicted observations relative to the as-deposited baseline, the boundaries over which those predictions should hold, the prior observations that support the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled low‐temperature annealing treatment applied to as‐deposited, non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi high‐entropy alloys will relieve internal strains and enhance short‐range chemical order (and possibly induce a moderate density of nanoscale features) at grain boundaries, thereby homogenizing the local magnetostructural transition. This homogenization is predicted to reduce the energy barriers associated with nucleation of the ferromagnetic phase during low‐applied-field cycling, resulting in a smoother (broadened) magnetocaloric response with reduced hysteresis compared to the as‐deposited state.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐deposited, ordered single‐phase hexagonal FeMnNiGeSi HEA that exhibits a sharp, first‐order magnetostructural transition with significant thermal hysteresis and limited heat exchange due to larger grain sizes and internal strain heterogeneities.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled low‐temperature annealing treatment (below the onset of the first‐order transition) designed to relieve local internal stresses and promote subtle short‐range chemical ordering.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under low-applied-field (approximately 0.5–1 T) magnetic-cooling cycles near the intrinsic transition temperature, ensuring that annealing conditions do not trigger unwanted phase transformations or excessive grain growth.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries and localized regions of chemical disorder/strain that, when modified by annealing, mediate the nucleation and growth of the ferromagnetic phase during the magnetostructural transition.
generation.mechanism: The low-temperature annealing relaxes residual internal stresses and enhances short-range ordering (and possibly promotes a moderate density of nanoscale precipitates), thereby reducing the dispersion in local transition temperatures. This homogenization lowers the energy barriers for domain reorientation during the phase transition, leading to a less abrupt, more distributed magnetocaloric change with reduced hysteresis.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as‐deposited baseline, the annealed samples are expected to exhibit a noticeably reduced thermal hysteresis and a broader, less abrupt magnetic entropy change profile (a smoother transition) during low-applied-field cycling, which should also enhance effective heat exchange.
generation.baseline: As‐deposited HEA samples showing a sharp, first‐order magnetostructural transition with high heterogeneity in local strain and chemical order leading to large hysteretic losses under low-field magnetic cooling cycles.
generation.boundary: This behavior is expected to hold for FeMnNiGeSi HEAs maintained in an ordered hexagonal state and subjected to moderate annealing that does not induce secondary phases, excessive coarsening, or compromise mechanical stability. Extreme annealing conditions or fields well outside the low-applied regime may produce different outcomes.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal annealing temperature and duration remain to be precisely defined, and slight variations in processing may affect the degree of strain relief and ordering, potentially altering the magnetocaloric response.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeMnNiGeSi HEA samples: one group remains in the as‐deposited state while the other is subjected to the controlled low‐temperature annealing treatment. Under identical low-applied-field (≈0.5–1 T) magnetic-cooling cycles, perform a comparative analysis of both groups. Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) or electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) to quantify changes in grain boundary density and local strain, and employ magnetometry to record magnetization versus temperature curves and hysteresis loops, as well as to derive the magnetic entropy change profile.
measurements: Grain boundary density and microstructural homogeneity (TEM/EBSD)
Hysteresis width from M–H curves under low-applied-field cycling
Assessment of short-range chemical order (e.g., via XRD or local-probe techniques)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in hysteresis width and a broadened, smoother ΔS versus temperature profile compared to the as‐deposited control, or if no clear correlation is found between modifications in grain boundary/strain characteristics and changes in the magnetocaloric response, then the hypothesis—that strain relief and enhanced short-range ordering mediate a reduced hysteretic magnetocaloric transition—is falsified.

The so-called “high entropy alloys” (HEAs) are a class of emergent transition metal alloys that hold great potential for advanced manufacturing, and which may impact magnetocalorics. These are near equimolar alloys with high entropy of mixing when in a random solid solution. These materials have been pursued for high hardness and resistance to wear and corrosion, which are attractive properties for a myriad of applications. Fe1Co1Ni1Cr1Pdx is an example HEA system with tunable magnetic properties. The addition of Pd was shown to change the critical temperature (Tc) from 300 to 500 K for x = 1 to 2, along with enhancement of the saturation magnetization; previous works have used high percentages of Pd as a stabilizing agent in similar high strength bulk alloys. In this work, we explore the magnetic properties of the Fe1Co1Ni1Cr1Pdx alloy family, as-rolled and after annealing, with low molar fractions of Pd. We find improvement in the magnetocaloric properties throughout the system. A detailed statistical analysis of the universal scaling behavior suggest this originates predominately from the homogenization of the alloy with both Pd and heat treatment. Most of the studies on magnetic and electrical properties of high entropy alloys focus on equiatomic FeCoCrNiX alloy (i.e., derivatives of the FeCoCrNiMn Cantor alloy) where X is Mn, Ti, Cu, or Pd and non-equiatomic FeCoCrNi with slight doping of Al, Cu, and Si. A wide spectrum of magnetic properties has been reported ranging from soft to semi-soft magnetic behavior in their coercivity. Among these alloys, the most studied single-phase FCC Cantor alloy exhibited multiple magnetic transitions from disordered paramagnetic phase to spin glass and subsequently to an ordered ferromagnetic state at low temperatures. More interestingly, the anti-invar property of this alloy which in turn induces strong magnetism in this alloy has been recently reported pointing to a potential for magnetism related applications. drafts.hypothesis: A controlled sub‐critical thermal annealing treatment will induce the formation of a moderate density of nanoscale precipitates within the ordered hexagonal phase of the as‐deposited, non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi HEA. These precipitates act as mediators that reduce domain boundary pinning during the magnetostructural transition, leading to a smoother (less abrupt) magnetocaloric entropy change and lower hysteretic losses under low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
drafts.material_initial_state: As-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi HEA realized via deposition techniques (arc-melted ingots or melt-spun microribbons) showing a single-phase ordered hexagonal structure with possible residual chemical heterogeneities.
drafts.intervention: Apply a controlled sub-critical thermal annealing treatment (in an inert atmosphere) designed to promote limited nanoscale precipitate formation without altering the primary hexagonal phase.
drafts.conditions: Annealing temperatures and durations are chosen to remain below any phase transformation or melting threshold, with experiments conducted near the standard magnetostructural transition temperature under low-applied-field cooling cycles.
drafts.structural_mediator: The induced nanoscale precipitates that modify the energy landscape of magnetostructural domain boundaries.
drafts.mechanism: Thermal activation via sub-critical annealing facilitates heterogeneous nucleation of nanoscale precipitates. These precipitates lower the domain boundary pinning energy and help distribute internal strains, thereby allowing a more gradual nucleation and growth of the magnetostructural transition, which reduces hysteresis while still enabling a substantial magnetocaloric effect.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-deposited baseline, annealed samples will exhibit a broader (less sharp) magnetocaloric entropy change with reduced hysteresis (narrower hysteresis loops), and potentially a slight shift (or smoothing) of the transition temperature. The improved microstructural uniformity should also enhance effective heat transfer due to smaller, more uniform domain evolution.
drafts.baseline: The as-deposited HEA, which exhibits a sharp, first-order magnetostructural transition with large but hysteretic entropy changes and relatively low surface-to-volume ratios limiting heat exchange rates.
drafts.boundary: This effect is expected to hold for FeMnNiGeSi-derived HEAs in which the primary phase remains the ordered hexagonal structure and for annealing conditions that do not induce secondary deleterious phases. Excessive annealing that leads to over-nucleation or coarsening, or substantial compositional segregation, may not follow this trend.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several batches of the as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi HEA and subject them to controlled annealing treatments with varied temperatures and durations that are below the phase transition thresholds. Characterize the microstructure (using TEM/SEM and XRD) to quantify nanoscale precipitate density and verify that the primary hexagonal phase is maintained. Measure the magnetocaloric response (e.g., entropy change via magnetometry) and hysteresis behavior during low-applied-field cooling cycles across all batches.
measurements: High-resolution TEM/SEM images to assess precipitate density and distribution
XRD measurements to confirm phase integrity
Magnetization vs temperature measurements under cyclic low-field conditions to extract entropy change profiles
Quantitative analysis of hysteresis loop areas from magnetization curves
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealing treatment does not result in a measurable change in precipitate density, or if any change in precipitate density is not correlated with the predicted smoother magnetocaloric transition and reduced hysteresis (or if an opposite trend is observed), then the hypothesis will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: The magnetocaloric response and hysteresis in as‐deposited, non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys are primarily governed by the distribution of localized lattice strains at grain boundaries that modulate the magnetostructural transition via magnetoelastic coupling.
drafts.material_initial_state: as-deposited, ordered single-phase hexagonal state obtained by typical deposition methods
drafts.intervention: Introduce a controlled post-deposition annealing step designed to induce a moderate and uniform nanocrystalline grain refinement without causing phase separation
drafts.conditions: Low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles with the requirement to maintain mechanical stability, low cost, and an increased effective surface-to-volume ratio for improved heat exchange
drafts.structural_mediator: Grain boundary density and associated local lattice strain distribution
drafts.mechanism: Enhanced grain boundary density reduces the average local strain energy barriers that control the nucleation and growth of the ferromagnetic phase during the magnetostructural transition. This diminution of the strain barrier enables a softer, less abrupt transition, thereby reducing hysteresis while still providing an appreciable magnetocaloric response.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-deposited baseline, the annealed specimens should exhibit a reduced thermal hysteresis width and a more gradual, broadened entropy change profile (even if the peak change is slightly moderated), indicating that the controlled increase in grain boundary density effectively modulates the magnetostructural transition.
drafts.baseline: as-deposited, ordered single-phase hexagonal FeMnNiGeSi-type alloy with larger grain sizes and comparatively higher hysteretic losses during low-applied-field cycles
drafts.boundary: This prediction should hold under low-field conditions relevant to magnetic cooling; the annealing intervention must be optimized so that the grain refinement is moderate and does not induce secondary phases or compromise mechanical stability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeMnNiGeSi-type alloy samples: one set as-deposited and a second set subjected to controlled post-deposition annealing to induce grain refinement. Subject both sets to identical low-applied-field magnetic cooling cycles. Characterize the samples by measuring grain size distribution (using EBSD or TEM), magnetization versus temperature curves, thermal hysteresis, and entropy change profiles.
measurements: Magnetization vs. temperature under low-applied fields
Entropy change as a function of temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not display a statistically significant reduction in thermal hysteresis and a correlated modification of the magnetocaloric profile relative to the as-deposited samples, or if no clear correlation is found between increased grain boundary density and performance change, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In the as‐deposited, non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi high‐entropy alloys, the sharp and hysteretic magnetocaloric response is primarily governed by a broad distribution of local magnetostructural transition temperatures arising from nanoscale chemical disorder and internal stresses. Mild, controlled low-temperature annealing that promotes short-range chemical ordering and relieves local strain will homogenize the transition, thereby reducing hysteresis and broadening the entropy change profile during low-field magnetic cooling cycles.
drafts.material_initial_state: As‐deposited FeMnNiGeSi HEA films or ribbons with a hexagonal ordered single phase but significant nanoscale chemical disorder and residual internal stresses due to rapid solidification.
drafts.intervention: Apply a controlled low-temperature annealing treatment (below the onset of the first-order magnetostructural transition) to promote subtle atomic rearrangements that increase short-range order without triggering full phase separation or coarsening.
drafts.conditions: Low-applied magnetic fields (e.g., on the order of 0.5 to 1 T) over a temperature range spanning the magnetostructural transition; experiments conducted on samples with high surface-to-volume ratios (e.g., thin films or microribbons) under cycling conditions that simulate magnetic refrigeration operation.
drafts.structural_mediator: Enhanced short-range chemical order and reduced local internal stresses (e.g., improved grain boundary uniformity) acting to narrow the distribution of local transition temperatures.
drafts.mechanism: The as-deposited state contains significant heterogeneity in composition and strain, which leads to a wide distribution of local magnetostructural transition temperatures and thereby produces a sharp but hysteretic entropy change. The annealing intervention relaxes internal stresses and promotes more uniform chemical ordering at the nanoscale, homogenizing the transition. This reduces energy barriers and narrows local differences, decreasing hysteresis and spreading out the caloric response over a broader temperature range.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-deposited baseline, annealed samples should exhibit a smoother (broadened) magnetocaloric transition with significantly reduced hysteresis width, potentially at the cost of a modest change in peak entropy change magnitude, but with enhanced heat transfer and cyclic stability.
drafts.baseline: As‐deposited alloys with a sharp, first-order magnetostructural transition that results in a large but hysteretic magnetic entropy change and limited heat-exchange rate due to low surface-to-volume characteristics.
drafts.boundary: This effect is expected under low-applied magnetic field conditions and for samples that maintain the hexagonal phase; results may vary if annealing is too aggressive, which could induce unwanted phase transformations or grain growth. The hypothesis applies specifically to non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi HEAs processed in a manner that retains high configurational disorder.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi HEA samples. Subject one set to a controlled low-temperature annealing treatment (optimized to promote short-range ordering without phase coarsening) while leaving the other set as-deposited. Under identical low-applied-field cycling conditions, measure and compare the magnetic entropy change as a function of temperature, hysteresis width (from M-H loops), and structural indicators (using X-ray diffraction and TEM) that signal changes in local ordering.
measurements: Magnetic entropy change (ΔS) vs. temperature under low-applied magnetic fields
Hysteresis width determined from field-cycling magnetization (M-H) measurements
Structural characterization via XRD and TEM to quantify short-range order and residual stresses
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in hysteresis width along with a broadened transition (i.e., a more gradual ΔS vs. temperature profile) relative to the as-deposited samples—or if the changes in structure do not correlate with reduced local compositional variability—then the hypothesis that short-range ordering mediated by annealing governs the reduced hysteresis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In as‐deposited, non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi HEAs, spatial variations in chemical order and lattice strain—especially localized at grain boundaries and free surfaces—govern the sharp first‐order magnetostructural transition and its associated hysteresis. Increasing the surface‐to‐volume ratio and refining the microstructure by controlled mechanical milling followed by a low‐temperature anneal should reduce internal strain heterogeneities and promote a more gradual (diffuse) magnetic transition with reduced hysteresis and an extended temperature window for the magnetocaloric response.
drafts.material_initial_state: As‐deposited non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi high‐entropy alloy with an ordered single‐phase hexagonal structure created by conventional arc melting or melt spinning (bulk or microribbons) exhibiting a sharp, first‐order magnetostructural transition with large but hysteretic entropy change and limited heat-exchange rate.
drafts.intervention: Apply a controlled high-energy mechanical milling process to produce a nanostructured, higher surface-area version of the alloy, followed by a low-temperature anneal to relieve excessive local stresses while preserving compositional heterogeneity.
drafts.conditions: Low-applied magnetic fields (e.g., ∼1 T or lower) during cooling cycles near the transition temperature; processing conditions should be tuned such that excessive grain coarsening is avoided but sufficient defect homogenization is achieved.
drafts.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries and free surfaces, where chemical disorder and lattice strain are most pronounced.
drafts.mechanism: The intervention reduces local strains and chemical inhomogeneity at surfaces and grain boundaries, which in turn broadens the distribution of exchange interactions. This leads to a more gradual magnetostructural transition with lower coercive fields (reduced hysteresis) and a broadened temperature range of significant entropy change, while also increasing the effective heat-exchange rate due to the higher surface-to-volume ratio.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-deposited baseline, nanostructured samples will exhibit a lower hysteresis loop width during low-field magnetic-cooling cycles and a broader, albeit slightly less sharp, magnetocaloric entropy change versus temperature profile, facilitating improved heat exchange.
drafts.baseline: Conventional, bulk or melt-spun samples with an ordered single-phase hexagonal structure that show a sharp, large, but hysteretic magnetocaloric response and lower heat-exchange rates.
drafts.boundary: These predictions are expected to hold under low-field (up to ∼1 T) magnetic-cooling cycles near the intrinsic magnetostructural transition temperature; extreme magnetic fields or significant alterations to the alloy’s overall phase (beyond the intended nanostructuring) may lead to different behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set is as-deposited (control) and the other set is processed via high-energy ball milling followed by a low-temperature anneal (intervention). Subject both sets to identical low-applied-field (∼1 T) magnetic-cooling cycles while monitoring the magnetic entropy change and hysteresis behavior as a function of temperature.
measurements: Magnetic hysteresis loops at various temperatures near the transition point
Temperature dependence of magnetic entropy change (ΔS) under adiabatic conditions
Microstructural characterization (grain size distribution, grain boundary density, and lattice strain via XRD and TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the intervention does not result in a measurable reduction in hysteresis width or fails to broaden the temperature range of the magnetocaloric response (i.e., the ΔS(T) curve remains as sharp as that of the control sample), then the proposed mechanism—that localized chemical disorder and strain at grain boundaries control the transition behavior—is falsified.
